Trap (B): Applying +1, +1, +2, +3 (miscounting O->P as +1 and A->C as +2) gives HPCO.
Trap (C): Shifting backward instead of forward (-1, -2, -3, -4) gives G-1 = F, O-2 = M, A-3 = X (wrapping past A), L-4 = H, so FMXH.
Trap (D): Applying +3 instead of +4 to the fourth letter (L(12)+3 = O(15)) gives HQDO.
questions.verify_code: answer = ''.join(chr(ord(c) + i + 1) for i, c in enumerate('GOAL'))

questions.question_text: In a certain code language, 'CAT' is coded as '24' and 'DOG' is coded as '26'. How will 'BAG' be coded in that language?
questions.trap_type: Multiplying instead of adding positional values
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: Each word is coded as the sum of the standard alphabetical positions (A=1, B=2, ..., Z=26) of its letters. For 'CAT': C(3) + A(1) + T(20) = 24. For 'DOG': D(4) + O(15) + G(7) = 26. Similarly, for 'BAG': B(2) + A(1) + G(7) = 10.
Trap (A): Multiplying the positional values instead of adding them (2 * 1 * 7) gives 14.
Trap (D): Using reverse alphabetical positions (Z=1, ..., B=25, A=26, G=20) and adding them (25 + 26 + 20) gives 71.
Trap (B): Concatenating B(2) and A(1) as 21 and ignoring G (or adding 11 to 10 by misreading G as Q=17) gives 21.

questions.question_text: Select the option that is related to the third number in the same way as the second number is related to the first number: 6 : 37 :: 8 : ?
questions.trap_type: Applying constant addition instead of squaring
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: The relationship between 6 and 37 is that the second number is 1 more than the square of the first number: 6^2 + 1 = 36 + 1 = 37. Applying the same rule to 8: 8^2 + 1 = 64 + 1 = 65.
Trap (B): Squaring 8 (8^2 = 64) and forgetting to add 1 gives 64.
Trap (A): Squaring 8 and subtracting 1 instead of adding 1 (8^2 - 1) gives 63.
Trap (C): Treating the relation as 6 * 6 + 1 = 37 and multiplying 8 by 6 plus 1 (8 * 6 + 1) gives 49.

questions.question_text: Select the word that is related to the third word in the same way as the second word is related to the first word: Thermometer : Temperature :: Odometer : ?
questions.trap_type: Confusing odometer with speedometer
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: The first word is a measuring instrument and the second word is the physical quantity it measures. A Thermometer measures Temperature. Similarly, an Odometer is an instrument used in vehicles to measure the Distance travelled.
Trap (D): Confusing an odometer with a speedometer (both are on a vehicle dashboard, and speedometer measures speed) gives Speed.
Trap (B): Confusing an odometer with a barometer or manometer (which measure pressure) gives Pressure.
Trap (C): Confusing an odometer with an ammeter (which measures electric current) gives Current.

questions.concept_tag: Odd One Out - Perfect Squares vs Cubes
questions.question_text: Four numbers have been given, out of which three are alike in some manner and one is different. Select the number that is different.
questions.trap_type: Divisibility or digit-sum distraction over square/cube property
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: Analyze the mathematical nature of the four numbers: 16 = 4^2 (perfect square), 25 = 5^2 (perfect square), 27 = 3^3 (perfect cube, not a square), and 36 = 6^2 (perfect square). Since 16, 25, and 36 are perfect squares while 27 is a perfect cube, 27 is the odd one out.
Trap (C): Noticing that 16 is a fourth power (2^4) while others are not gives 16.
Trap (B): Noticing that 25 is a multiple of 5 while 16, 27, 36 are not gives 25.
Trap (A): Noticing that 36 is divisible by both 2 and 3 (or 6) unlike the others gives 36.

questions.concept_tag: Odd One Out - Letter Cluster Gaps
questions.question_text: Three of the following four letter-clusters are alike in a certain way and one is different. Pick the odd one out.
questions.trap_type: Miscounting the gap between letters
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Write the alphabetical positions: B(2)-D(4) = +2, J(10)-L(12) = +2, N(14)-P(16) = +2, but S(19)-V(22) = +3. BD, JL and NP each skip exactly one letter (C, K, O), while SV skips two (T, U). So SV is the odd one out. Trap (C): BD is the only cluster whose letter positions are single-digit numbers, a surface feature that is not the pattern. Trap (A): JL is picked by miscounting J-K-L as a gap of two letters. Trap (B): NP is picked by miscounting N-O-P as +3.
questions.verify_code: answer = [k for k, v in {'C': 'BD', 'D': 'SV', 'A': 'JL', 'B': 'NP'}.items() if ord(v[1]) - ord(v[0]) != 2][0]

questions.question_text: A is the brother of B. B is the mother of C. D is the father of A. How is D related to C?
questions.trap_type: Paternal vs Maternal lineage confusion
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: Trace the family tree generation by generation. 1) B is the mother of C (B is female, one generation above C). 2) A is the brother of B (so A is C's maternal uncle, and A and B are siblings). 3) D is the father of A. Since A and B are siblings, D is also the father of B. Because B is C's mother, B's father D is C's Maternal Grandfather.
Trap (D): Skipping a generation and reading D as the father of C instead of A/B gives Father.
Trap (A): Identifying D as a grandfather correctly but forgetting that B is the mother (female) rather than the father gives Paternal Grandfather.
Trap (C): Confusing D's relation to C with A's relation to C (A is C's maternal uncle) gives Maternal Uncle.

questions.concept_tag: Blood Relations - Pointing to a Person
questions.question_text: Pointing to a boy, Rina said, "He is the son of the only son of my paternal grandfather." How is that boy related to Rina?
questions.trap_type: Reversing generation or ignoring 'only son' constraint
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Rina's paternal grandfather is her father's father. His only son is therefore Rina's father. The son of Rina's father is Rina's brother. Trap (B): Son reads "the son of the only son" as if the only son were Rina herself or her husband. Trap (A): Cousin treats the grandfather's only son as Rina's uncle, but the only son of a paternal grandfather must be her father. Trap (D): Nephew treats the only son as Rina's brother, skipping one generation.

questions.question_text: Rohan walks 10 m North, then turns right and walks 15 m, and then turns right again and walks 10 m. How far and in which direction is he now from his starting point?
questions.trap_type: Reference point reversal (Starting point from End point)
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: Let the starting point be the origin (0, 0). 1) Rohan walks 10 m North to reach (0, 10). 2) Facing North, he turns right (which is East) and walks 15 m to reach (15, 10). 3) Facing East, he turns right again (which is South) and walks 10 m to reach (15, 0). The northward 10 m and southward 10 m cancel each other out. He is now at (15, 0), which is 15 m East of his starting point (0, 0).
Trap (C): Confusing right turns with left turns (or finding the direction of the starting point from his final position) gives 15 m West.
Trap (D): Adding the last two segments (15 m + 10 m) instead of cancelling the vertical movements gives 25 m East.
Trap (A): Adding total distance walked (10 + 15 + 10 = 35 m) instead of finding net displacement gives 35 m East.

questions.question_text: Priya is facing East. She turns 90 degrees clockwise, and then turns 180 degrees anticlockwise. Which direction is she facing now?
questions.trap_type: Swapping clockwise and anticlockwise rotations
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: 1) Priya starts facing East. 2) Turning 90 degrees clockwise from East moves her to face South. 3) Turning 180 degrees anticlockwise (or in any direction) reverses her facing direction to the exact opposite of South, which is North. Alternatively, net rotation = 90° CW - 180° ACW = 90° ACW from East = North.
Trap (B): Swapping clockwise and anticlockwise (turning 90° ACW to North, then 180° CW to South) or stopping after the first turn gives South.
Trap (A): Applying the 180° turn from the initial direction (East -> West) while ignoring the 90° turn gives West.
Trap (C): Treating 180° as a full circle back to the original direction gives East.

questions.concept_tag: Ranking and Order - Finding Opposite Rank
questions.question_text: In a class of 40 students, Neha ranks 15th from the top. What is her rank from the bottom?
questions.trap_type: Forgetting to add 1 when subtracting rank from total
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: When the total number of students and rank from one end are given, the rank from the other end is calculated as: (Total - Given Rank) + 1. Subtracting 15 from 40 gives the 25 students below Neha. Adding 1 for Neha herself gives her rank from the bottom: (40 - 15) + 1 = 25 + 1 = 26th.
Trap (A): Subtracting 15 from 40 directly (40 - 15 = 25) without adding 1 gives the number of students below her rather than her rank (25th).
Trap (B): Subtracting 1 instead of adding 1 (40 - 15 - 1 = 24) gives 24th.
Trap (C): Adding 2 instead of 1 due to inclusive counting error (40 - 15 + 2) gives 27th.

questions.question_text:
Statements:
1. All pens are books.
2. All books are tables.
Conclusions:
I. All pens are tables.
II. All tables are pens.
Which of the following options is correct?

options.C: Both Conclusions I and II follow
options.D: Neither Conclusion I nor II follows

questions.trap_type: Illicit conversion of universal affirmative ('All A are B' -> 'All B are A')
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: In a Venn diagram, the circle for 'Pens' is completely inside the circle for 'Books', and the circle for 'Books' is completely inside the circle for 'Tables'. Therefore, the circle for 'Pens' is completely inside 'Tables', so Conclusion I ("All pens are tables") definitely follows. However, the outer circle 'Tables' can have area outside 'Pens', so Conclusion II ("All tables are pens") does not definitely follow. Only Conclusion I follows.
Trap (A): Reversing the subset direction (thinking the outer circle is inside the inner circle) gives Only Conclusion II follows.
Trap (C): Assuming 'All A are B' means the sets A and B are identical (so 'All tables are pens' is also true) gives Both Conclusions I and II follow.
Trap (D): Thinking that since 'pens' and 'tables' are not in the same single statement, no definite relation exists between them gives Neither Conclusion I nor II follows.

questions.concept_tag: Seating Arrangement - Linear Row Facing North
questions.question_text: Five friends P, Q, R, S, and T are sitting in a row facing North. S is at the extreme left end. P is sitting at the exact center of the row. Q is to the immediate left of P. T is to the immediate right of P. Who is sitting at the extreme right end?
questions.trap_type: Confusing 'immediate right of center' with 'extreme right end'
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: Draw 5 positions from left to right (1, 2, 3, 4, 5) facing North. 1) S is at the extreme left end -> Position 1 is S. 2) P is at the exact center -> Position 3 is P. 3) Q is to the immediate left of P -> Position 2 is Q. 4) T is to the immediate right of P -> Position 4 is T. 5) Only Position 5 (the extreme right end) remains empty, so the remaining person R sits at Position 5. Order: S - Q - P - T - R. Thus, R is at the extreme right end.
Trap (A): Reversing left and right for North-facing persons and placing Q on the right gives Q.
Trap (D): Mistaking T (who is the rightmost person explicitly placed in the clues at Position 4) as the extreme right end gives T.
Trap (B): Misreading 'exact center' as the end position gives P.

questions.question_text: Four friends P, Q, R and S are sitting around a circular table facing the centre. Q is sitting to the immediate right of P. R is sitting opposite to P. Who is sitting to the immediate left of P?
questions.trap_type: Facing-center vs Facing-outward left/right reversal
questions.pedagogical_explanation: With 4 seats, each person has one neighbour on the right, one on the left and one person opposite. Q is P's immediate right and R is opposite P, so the only seat left, P's immediate left, belongs to S. Trap (D): R is opposite P, not next to P. Trap (A): Q gets the answer by reversing left and right, as though the friends faced outward. Trap (B): "Cannot be determined" assumes more clues are needed, but with only 4 seats the last seat is fixed.

questions.question_text: Six executives—P, Q, R, S, T, and U—are sitting in a straight row facing South. S sits second from the East end of the row. T sits second to the right of S. Only one person sits between T and P. Q sits to the immediate left of P, and R does not sit at any extreme end of the row. Who is sitting to the immediate left of T?
questions.trap_type: Confusing left and right when all persons face South
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Step-by-step: Number the 6 seats from West to East as 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6. Because everyone faces South, a person's right is towards the West (lower seat number) and their left is towards the East (higher seat number). S sits second from the East end, so S = Seat 5. T sits second to the right (West) of S, so T = Seat 3. Only one person sits between T (Seat 3) and P; since Seat 5 is occupied by S, P must be at Seat 1. Q sits to the immediate left (East) of P, so Q = Seat 2. Between the remaining Seats 4 and 6, R does not sit at an extreme end, so R = Seat 4 and U = Seat 6. The West-to-East arrangement is P - Q - T - R - S - U. Facing South, the person to the immediate left (East) of T (Seat 3) is at Seat 4, which is R. Trap (B): Treating 'immediate left of T' as West (North-facing orientation) instead of East gives Q at Seat 2. Trap (C): Reading 'immediate left of T' as 'second to the left of T' gives S at Seat 5. Trap (D): Overlooking the clue that R does not sit at an extreme end and placing U at Seat 4 gives U.
questions.verify_code:
import itertools
sols = []
for p in itertools.permutations('PQRSTU'):
    s = {c: i + 1 for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    if s['S'] != 5: continue
    if s['T'] != s['S'] - 2: continue
    if abs(s['T'] - s['P']) != 2: continue
    if s['Q'] != s['P'] + 1: continue
    if s['R'] in (1, 6): continue
    sols.append(p)
assert len(sols) == 1
p = sols[0]
answer = p[p.index('T') + 1]

questions.question_text: Seven doctors—K, L, M, N, O, P, and Q—are sitting around a circular table facing the center. L sits third to the right of K. N sits to the immediate left of L. M sits to the immediate left of K. O sits to the immediate right of P. Who sits to the immediate right of K?
questions.trap_type: Confusing immediate left and immediate right on a circle
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Step-by-step: Number the 7 seats from 1 to 7 in counter-clockwise order (which corresponds to moving to the right when facing the center). Place K at Seat 1. L sits third to the right of K, so L = Seat 4. N sits to the immediate left (clockwise) of L, so N = Seat 3. M sits to the immediate left (clockwise) of K, so M = Seat 7. The remaining empty seats are 2, 5, and 6. Since O sits to the immediate right of P, P and O must occupy two consecutive counter-clockwise seats, which can only be P = Seat 5 and O = Seat 6. This leaves Q for Seat 2. Therefore, the person sitting to the immediate right of K (Seat 2) is Q. Trap (A): Taking 'second to the right of K' (Seat 3) instead of 'immediate right of K' gives N. Trap (D): Misplacing N to the immediate right of L (Seat 5), which forces the consecutive pair P and O into Seats 2 and 3, gives P at Seat 2. Trap (C): Confusing 'immediate right of K' with 'immediate left of K' (Seat 7) gives M.
questions.verify_code:
import itertools
sols = []
for p in itertools.permutations('LMNOPQ'):
    seat = dict(zip('K' + ''.join(p), range(7)))
    r = lambda x, k: (seat[x] + k) % 7
    if seat['L'] != r('K', 3): continue
    if seat['N'] != r('L', -1): continue
    if seat['M'] != r('K', -1): continue
    if seat['O'] != r('P', 1): continue
    sols.append(seat)
assert len(sols) == 1
inv = {v: k for k, v in sols[0].items()}
answer = inv[(sols[0]['K'] + 1) % 7]

questions.question_text: Six people—E, F, G, H, I, and J—live on six different floors of a building numbered 1 to 6 from bottom to top. H lives on Floor 4. Only two people live between H and E. F lives immediately above G, and G lives on an even-numbered floor. I lives on an even-numbered floor. Who lives on Floor 5?
questions.trap_type: Placing I on Floor 5 by overlooking that I must live on an even-numbered floor
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Step-by-step: Number the floors from 1 (bottom) to 6 (top). H lives on Floor 4. Since two people live between H (Floor 4) and E, E must live on Floor 1. F lives immediately above G and G is on an even-numbered floor; the remaining even floors are Floor 2 and Floor 6. G cannot be on Floor 6 because F lives immediately above G, so G = Floor 2 and F = Floor 3. Now only Floors 5 and 6 remain for I and J. Since I lives on an even-numbered floor, I = Floor 6, which leaves J on Floor 5. Trap (D): Ignoring the clue that I lives on an even-numbered floor and placing I on Floor 5 gives I. Trap (C): Reversing 'F lives immediately above G' to 'G lives immediately above F' puts G on even Floor 6 and F on Floor 5, giving F. Trap (A): Ignoring the clue that G lives on an even-numbered floor allows G = Floor 5 with F = Floor 6, giving G.
questions.verify_code:
import itertools
sols = []
for p in itertools.permutations('EFGHIJ'):
    f = {c: i + 1 for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    if f['H'] != 4 or abs(f['H'] - f['E']) != 3: continue
    if f['F'] != f['G'] + 1 or f['G'] % 2: continue
    if f['I'] % 2: continue
    sols.append(p)
assert len(sols) == 1
answer = sols[0][4]

questions.question_text: Five boxes—P, Q, R, S, and T—are stacked one above the other from position 1 (bottom) to position 5 (top). Box R is placed at the exact middle position. Only one box is placed between R and P. Box S is placed immediately above Box Q, and Box Q is not at the bottom position. Which box is at the bottom position (position 1)?
questions.trap_type: Placing P at the top (position 5) and forcing Q into the bottom position
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Step-by-step: Number the stack positions from 1 (bottom) to 5 (top). Box R is in the middle, so R = Position 3. Since one box is between R (Position 3) and P, P can be at Position 1 or Position 5. Box S is immediately above Box Q, requiring two consecutive empty positions—either (1, 2) or (4, 5). However, Q is not at Position 1 (bottom), so Q and S cannot occupy Positions 1 and 2. Therefore, Q = Position 4 and S = Position 5. Consequently, P must occupy Position 1 (bottom), and the remaining Box T occupies Position 2. Thus, Box P is at the bottom position. Trap (B): Overlooking the constraint that Q is not at the bottom position and placing (Q, S) at Positions (1, 2) gives Q. Trap (A): Reversing 'S is immediately above Q' to 'Q is immediately above S' at Positions (1, 2) gives S at Position 1. Trap (D): Confusing Position 2 with Position 1 after placing P at Position 1 gives T.
questions.verify_code:
import itertools
sols = []
for p in itertools.permutations('PQRST'):
    f = {c: i + 1 for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    if f['R'] != 3 or abs(f['R'] - f['P']) != 2: continue
    if f['S'] != f['Q'] + 1 or f['Q'] == 1: continue
    sols.append(p)
assert len(sols) == 1
answer = sols[0][0]

questions.question_text: If 'X + Y' means 'X is the father of Y', 'X - Y' means 'X is the mother of Y', 'X * Y' means 'X is the brother of Y', and 'X / Y' means 'X is the sister of Y', then in the expression 'P + Q * R - S', how is Q related to S?
questions.trap_type: Confusing maternal uncle with paternal uncle by misreading R as the father of S
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Step-by-step: Decode the expression from left to right: 'P + Q' means P is the father of Q; 'Q * R' means Q is the brother of R (so Q is male); 'R - S' means R is the mother of S. Since Q is the brother of S's mother (R), Q is the Maternal Uncle of S. Trap (A): Misreading 'R - S' as 'R is the father of S' makes Q the father's brother, giving Paternal Uncle. Trap (C): Misreading 'Q * R' as Q being the husband of R gives Father. Trap (B): Stopping at the relation between Q and R ('Q is the brother of R') instead of finding Q's relation to S gives Brother.

questions.question_text: In a family of six members—K, L, M, N, O, and P—K is the paternal grandfather of P. M is the father of P and the brother of N. L is the mother of P. O is the mother of M. How is O related to L?
questions.trap_type: Reversing the subject and object of the relationship question
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Step-by-step: M is the father of P and L is the mother of P, which means M and L are a married couple (M is the husband, L is the wife). O is the mother of M, and K is the paternal grandfather of P (so K and O are the parents of M and N). Since O is the mother of L's husband (M), O is the Mother-in-law of L. Trap (C): Confusing L (the wife of M) with N (the sibling of M), which makes O her biological Mother. Trap (D): Answering 'How is L related to O?' (Daughter-in-law) instead of 'How is O related to L?'. Trap (B): Answering O's relation to P (Grandmother) instead of O's relation to L.

questions.concept_tag: Multi-Turn Direction Sense and Shortest Distance
questions.question_text: Rohan starts from Point X and walks 12 meters North to Point Y. He then turns right and walks 9 meters to Point Z. Next, he turns right again and walks 4 meters to Point W, and finally turns left and walks 6 meters to reach Point V. What is the shortest straight-line distance between Point X and Point V?
questions.trap_type: Turning West instead of East on the final left turn while facing South
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Step-by-step: Set Point X at the origin (0, 0). Walking 12m North to Y puts him at (0, 12). Turning right (East) and walking 9m to Z puts him at (9, 12). Turning right (South) and walking 4m to W reduces his Northward displacement to 12 - 4 = 8m, putting him at (9, 8) facing South. From South, a left turn is towards the East, so walking 6m East to V increases his Eastward displacement to 9 + 6 = 15m, putting him at (15, 8). By Pythagoras' theorem, shortest distance XV = sqrt(15^2 + 8^2) = sqrt(225 + 64) = sqrt(289) = 17 meters. Trap (A): Turning West instead of East on the final left turn puts V at (9 - 6, 8) = (3, 8), giving sqrt(3^2 + 8^2) = √73 meters. Trap (B): Stopping at Point Z and calculating the hypotenuse XZ = sqrt(12^2 + 9^2) = 15 meters. Trap (D): Adding the net horizontal and vertical displacements (15 + 8 = 23 meters) instead of applying Pythagoras' theorem.
questions.verify_code:
x, y = 0, 0
d = (0, 1)
right = lambda v: (v[1], -v[0])
left = lambda v: (-v[1], v[0])
x, y = x + 12 * d[0], y + 12 * d[1]
d = right(d); x, y = x + 9 * d[0], y + 9 * d[1]
d = right(d); x, y = x + 4 * d[0], y + 4 * d[1]
d = left(d); x, y = x + 6 * d[0], y + 6 * d[1]
answer = (x * x + y * y) ** 0.5

questions.concept_tag: Shadow and Direction Sense at Sunrise
questions.question_text: One morning just after sunrise, Kavita and Meenal were standing in a park facing each other and talking. If Kavita's shadow fell exactly to the right of Meenal, in which direction was Kavita facing?
questions.trap_type: Reporting the direction Meenal was facing instead of Kavita
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Step-by-step: At sunrise, the sun is in the East, so all shadows fall towards the West. Since Kavita's shadow falls to the right of Meenal, Meenal's right-hand side must be West. A person whose right hand points West must be facing South. Therefore, Meenal is facing South. Since Kavita and Meenal are facing each other, Kavita is facing North. Trap (D): Stopping after finding the direction Meenal is facing (South) instead of Kavita's facing direction. Trap (B): Assuming that because the sun rises in the East, Kavita is facing East. Trap (A): Assuming Kavita is facing the direction of her shadow (West).
questions.verify_code:
dirs = ['North', 'East', 'South', 'West']
shadow = 'West'
m = [f for f in dirs if dirs[(dirs.index(f) + 1) % 4] == shadow][0]

questions.concept_tag: Syllogism with 'Only a Few' and Possibility
questions.question_text: Statements: I. Only a few rivers are lakes. II. All lakes are oceans. Conclusions: 1. All rivers being oceans is a possibility. 2. Some rivers are definitely not lakes.
questions.trap_type: Treating 'Only a few rivers are lakes' as simple 'Some rivers are lakes' or extending the restriction to oceans
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Step-by-step: 'Only a few rivers are lakes' means two things simultaneously: 'Some rivers are lakes' AND 'Some rivers are NOT lakes'. Therefore, Conclusion 2 ('Some rivers are definitely not lakes') directly follows. Furthermore, while some rivers cannot be inside 'Lakes', the 'Oceans' circle contains 'Lakes' and can expand to encompass the entire 'Rivers' circle without forcing all rivers into 'Lakes'. Thus, Conclusion 1 ('All rivers being oceans is a possibility') also follows. Hence, both conclusions 1 and 2 follow. Trap (D): Treating 'Only a few A are B' as ordinary 'Some A are B' and rejecting Conclusion 2. Trap (A): Assuming that because some rivers cannot be lakes, those rivers cannot be oceans either, and rejecting Conclusion 1. Trap (C): Rejecting both possibility and negative deductions from 'Only a few'.

questions.concept_tag: Syllogism with Universal Negative and Possibility
questions.question_text: Statements: I. All clouds are rains. II. No rain is mist. Conclusions: 1. No cloud is mist. 2. Some clouds being mist is a possibility.
questions.trap_type: Treating a contradictory definite false statement as a valid possibility or an either-or pair
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Step-by-step: Since the 'Clouds' circle lies entirely inside the 'Rains' circle, and 'Rains' has zero overlap with 'Mist', 'Clouds' can never overlap with 'Mist'. Thus, Conclusion 1 ('No cloud is mist') is 100% definitely true. Because 'No cloud is mist' is definitely true, any overlap between clouds and mist is impossible, making Conclusion 2 ('Some clouds being mist is a possibility') definitely false. Therefore, only conclusion 1 follows. Trap (A): Assuming that any conclusion containing the word 'possibility' is automatically true. Trap (B): Seeing the complementary pair 'No cloud is mist' and 'Some clouds are mist' and selecting 'Either 1 or 2 follows', forgetting that either-or only applies when neither conclusion is definitely true on its own. Trap (D): Accepting both the definite negative and the positive possibility simultaneously.

questions.question_text: Statements: P > Q >= R = S; S <= T < U. Conclusions: 1. P > S  2. R < U
questions.trap_type: Rejecting a strict inequality when >= or <= appears alongside > or < in the chain
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Step-by-step: Combine the two statements through the common element S: P > Q >= R = S <= T < U. For Conclusion 1 (P to S): the chain is P > Q >= R = S. Since there is at least one strict '>' sign in the same direction, P > S is definitely true. For Conclusion 2 (R to U): the chain is R = S <= T < U. Since there is a strict '<' sign between T and U in the same direction, R < U is definitely true. Thus, both conclusions 1 and 2 follow. Trap (A): Thinking that 'S <= T' blocks the strict inequality 'R < U' and accepting only Conclusion 1. Trap (D): Thinking that 'Q >= R' weakens 'P > Q' to 'P >= S' and accepting only Conclusion 2. Trap (C): Assuming that '>' and '<' in the combined chain always cancel out, even when conclusions are tested on separate halves of the chain.

questions.question_text: In a certain code language, every consonant in a word is replaced by the third letter following it (+3) in the English alphabet, and every vowel is replaced by the second letter preceding it (-2) in the English alphabet. How will the word 'CROWN' be written in that code language?
questions.trap_type: Applying the +3 consonant shift to the vowel 'O' as well
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Step-by-step: Identify consonants and vowels in 'CROWN': C(3), R(18), W(23), and N(14) are consonants (+3 shift), while O(15) is a vowel (-2 shift). Applying the rules: C(3)+3 = F(6); R(18)+3 = U(21); O(15)-2 = M(13); W(23)+3 = Z(26); N(14)+3 = Q(17). Combining these letters gives FUMZQ. Trap (D): Applying the +3 consonant shift to all letters including the vowel O (O(15)+3 = R(18)) produces FURZQ. Trap (B): Adding 2 instead of subtracting 2 for the vowel O (O(15)+2 = Q(17)) produces FUQZQ. Trap (A): Swapping the rules (subtracting 2 from consonants and adding 3 to vowels) produces APRUL.
questions.verify_code: answer = ''.join(chr(ord(c) - 2) if c in 'AEIOU' else chr(ord(c) + 3) for c in 'CROWN')

questions.question_text: In a certain code language, 'SILVER' is written as 'JTWMSF'. How will 'PLANET' be written in that language?
questions.trap_type: Shifting letters by +1 without swapping adjacent pairs first
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Step-by-step: Divide the 6-letter word into three adjacent pairs, swap the two letters within each pair, and then shift every letter forward by +1. For 'SILVER': pairs (SI)(LV)(ER) swap to (IS)(VL)(RE), and shifting each letter by +1 gives JTWMSF. Applying the same two-step pattern to 'PLANET': pairs (PL)(AN)(ET) swap to (LP)(NA)(TE). Shifting each letter by +1 gives L+1=M, P+1=Q, N+1=O, A+1=B, T+1=U, and E+1=F, resulting in MQOBUF. Trap (B): Shifting each letter of 'PLANET' by +1 directly without swapping adjacent pairs produces QMBOFU. Trap (D): Swapping the adjacent pairs of 'PLANET' to get LPNATE but forgetting to add +1 to each letter. Trap (C): Swapping adjacent pairs and subtracting 1 (-1) instead of adding 1 (+1) produces KOMZSD.
questions.verify_code:
w = 'PLANET'
sw = ''.join(w[i + 1] + w[i] for i in range(0, len(w), 2))
answer = ''.join(chr(ord(c) + 1) for c in sw)

questions.question_text: Select the number that will replace the question mark (?) in the following series: 5, 11, 21, 43, 85, ?
questions.trap_type: Applying ×2 - 1 instead of alternating ×2 + 1 and ×2 - 1
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Step-by-step: Examine how each term is generated from the previous term: 5 * 2 + 1 = 11; 11 * 2 - 1 = 21; 21 * 2 + 1 = 43; 43 * 2 - 1 = 85. The pattern alternates between (×2 + 1) and (×2 - 1). Since the last operation was (×2 - 1), the next operation must be (×2 + 1): 85 * 2 + 1 = 171. Trap (A): Repeating the previous step's (×2 - 1) operation instead of alternating to (×2 + 1) gives 85 * 2 - 1 = 169. Trap (D): Doubling 85 to 170 and forgetting the +1 offset. Trap (C): Repeating the last difference (85 - 43 = 42) and computing 85 + 42 = 127.

questions.question_text: Find the missing number in the series: 14, 20, 44, 104, 224, ?
questions.trap_type: Adding 6^3 without subtracting 6, or assuming a constant second-order difference
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Step-by-step: Calculate the differences between consecutive terms: 20 - 14 = 6; 44 - 20 = 24; 104 - 44 = 60; 224 - 104 = 120. These differences follow the pattern (n^3 - n) for n = 2, 3, 4, 5: 2^3 - 2 = 6; 3^3 - 3 = 24; 4^3 - 4 = 60; 5^3 - 5 = 120. For the next step (n = 6), the difference is 6^3 - 6 = 216 - 6 = 210. Adding this to 224 gives 224 + 210 = 434. Trap (C): Repeating the last difference of 120 gives 224 + 120 = 344. Trap (D): Repeating the last second-order difference (120 - 60 = 60) so the next difference is 120 + 60 = 180, giving 224 + 180 = 404. Trap (B): Adding the full cube 6^3 = 216 without subtracting 6 gives 224 + 216 = 440.

questions.question_text: In a row of cadets facing North, Vikram is 15th from the left end and Rakesh is 18th from the right end. When they interchange their positions, Vikram becomes 22nd from the left end. How many cadets are there in the row?
questions.trap_type: Adding new left rank and old right rank without subtracting 1
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Step-by-step: After interchanging positions, Vikram moves to Rakesh's original seat. Therefore, Rakesh's original seat is both 22nd from the left end (Vikram's new position) and 18th from the right end (Rakesh's original position). Using the total formula on this single seat: Total cadets = (Left rank + Right rank) - 1 = 22 + 18 - 1 = 39. Trap (D): Adding 22 + 18 = 40 and forgetting to subtract 1 for counting the same seat from both ends. Trap (A): Subtracting 2 instead of 1 (22 + 18 - 2 = 38). Trap (C): Adding Vikram's old left rank and Rakesh's old right rank (15 + 18 - 1 = 32) instead of using Vikram's new rank after the swap.

questions.question_text: A number-arrangement machine rearranges a given input step by step by moving the smallest unarranged number to the extreme left end in each step while shifting the remaining numbers one position to the right. Input: 48  19  63  12  35  27. Which of the following will be Step III for the given input?
questions.trap_type: Placing newly arranged numbers in ascending order from the left instead of prepending each to the extreme left end
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Step-by-step: In each step, the machine moves the smallest unarranged number to the EXTREME LEFT end (prepend), pushing previously arranged numbers to the right. Input: 48  19  63  12  35  27. Step I (smallest is 12, moved to extreme left): 12  48  19  63  35  27. Step II (next smallest is 19, moved to extreme left ahead of 12): 19  12  48  63  35  27. Step III (next smallest is 27, moved to extreme left ahead of 19): 27  19  12  48  63  35. Trap (C): Placing each arranged number after the previously arranged numbers in ascending order (12, then 19, then 27) instead of at the extreme left end gives 12  19  27  48  63  35. Trap (B): Sorting the entire array in a single step gives 12  19  27  35  48  63. Trap (A): Stopping at Step II instead of completing Step III gives 19  12  48  63  35  27.
questions.verify_code:
a = [48, 19, 63, 12, 35, 27]
done = []
for step in range(3):
    rest = [x for x in a if x not in done]
    m = min(rest)
    done.append(m)
    a = [m] + [x for x in a if x != m]
ans = '  '.join(str(x) for x in a)
OPTS = {'C': '12  19  27  48  63  35', 'B': '12  19  27  35  48  63', 'D': '27  19  12  48  63  35', 'A': '19  12  48  63  35  27'}
answer = [k for k, v in OPTS.items() if v == ans][0]

questions.question_text: Statement: Despite a 30% increase in the government subsidy on rooftop solar panels this year, residential adoption in Tier-2 cities has grown by less than 4%, largely due to lengthy bank loan approval processes and a shortage of certified local installers. Conclusions: 1. Financial subsidy alone is not sufficient to drive rapid residential solar adoption in Tier-2 cities. 2. Completely abolishing the rooftop solar subsidy will immediately increase residential solar adoption in Tier-2 cities.
questions.trap_type: Assuming that because a subsidy was insufficient on its own, removing it would reverse the problem
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Step-by-step: The statement explicitly notes that even with a 30% higher subsidy, growth remained below 4% because of procedural (loan approval) and operational (installer shortage) bottlenecks. This directly supports Conclusion 1: financial subsidy by itself is not sufficient to drive rapid adoption. Conclusion 2 is illogical and contradicts the premise, as abolishing the subsidy does not fix loan delays or installer shortages. Therefore, only conclusion 1 follows. Trap (D): Selecting the extreme contrarian conclusion (Conclusion 2) while ignoring the direct inference in Conclusion 1. Trap (B): Accepting Conclusion 2 alongside Conclusion 1. Trap (C): Rejecting Conclusion 1 by thinking the word 'not sufficient' goes beyond the statement.

questions.concept_tag: Linear Seating Arrangement - Single Row Facing North
questions.question_text: Six executives—Aarav, Bhavya, Charan, Divya, Esha, and Farhan—are sitting in a straight row facing North, not necessarily in the same order. Divya sits third from the right end. Only one person sits between Divya and Farhan. Bhavya sits to the immediate left of Farhan. Aarav sits second to the left of Bhavya. Charan does not sit at any of the extreme ends of the row. Who sits second to the right of Aarav?
questions.trap_type: Counting the wrong number of seats or the wrong direction from the reference person
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: Number the six North-facing seats 1 to 6 from left to right. 1) Divya sits third from the right end, so Divya is at Seat 4. 2) Only one person sits between Divya and Farhan, so Farhan is at Seat 2 or Seat 6. 3) Bhavya sits to the immediate left of Farhan. If Farhan were at Seat 2, Bhavya would be at Seat 1 and Aarav (second to the left of Bhavya) would have no seat, so Farhan is at Seat 6 and Bhavya at Seat 5. 4) Aarav sits second to the left of Bhavya, so Aarav is at Seat 3. 5) Charan is not at an extreme end, so Charan is at Seat 2 and Esha at Seat 1. Final row (left to right): Esha, Charan, Aarav, Divya, Bhavya, Farhan. Second to the right of Aarav (Seat 3) is Seat 5, which is Bhavya.
Trap (D): Moving two seats to the left of Aarav instead of the right lands on Seat 1, giving Esha.
Trap (C): Moving only one seat (immediate right) instead of two lands on Seat 4, giving Divya.
Trap (A): Taking the immediate left of Aarav instead of second to the right lands on Seat 2, giving Charan.
questions.verify_code:
import itertools
sols = []
for p in itertools.permutations(['Aarav', 'Bhavya', 'Charan', 'Divya', 'Esha', 'Farhan']):
    s = {n: i + 1 for i, n in enumerate(p)}
    if s['Divya'] != 4: continue
    if abs(s['Divya'] - s['Farhan']) != 2: continue
    if s['Bhavya'] != s['Farhan'] - 1: continue
    if s['Aarav'] != s['Bhavya'] - 2: continue
    if s['Charan'] in (1, 6): continue
    sols.append(p)
assert len(sols) == 1
p = sols[0]
answer = p[p.index('Aarav') + 2]

questions.question_text: Six doctors—Gaurav, Harish, Indu, Jatin, Kavya, and Lalit—are sitting around a circular table facing the center. Gaurav sits second to the right of Indu. Only two persons sit between Gaurav and Kavya. Harish sits to the immediate left of Kavya. Jatin is not an immediate neighbour of Indu. Who sits to the immediate right of Jatin?
questions.trap_type: Reading the wrong neighbour (left vs right, or the wrong number of seats) in a centre-facing circle
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: For people facing the centre, 'right' is anticlockwise. Number the six seats 0 to 5 anticlockwise, so moving right is +1 and moving left is -1. 1) Place Indu at Seat 0. 2) Gaurav sits second to the right of Indu, so Gaurav is at Seat 2. 3) Only two persons sit between Gaurav and Kavya; in a 6-seat circle this means they sit opposite each other, so Kavya is at Seat 5. 4) Harish sits to the immediate left of Kavya, so Harish is at Seat 4. 5) Seats 1 and 3 remain. Seat 1 is next to Indu, and Jatin is not an immediate neighbour of Indu, so Jatin is at Seat 3 and Lalit at Seat 1. The immediate right of Jatin (Seat 3 + 1) is Seat 4, which is Harish.
Trap (D): Taking the immediate left of Jatin (Seat 2) instead of the immediate right gives Gaurav.
Trap (C): Taking the person sitting opposite Jatin (Seat 0) instead of the immediate right gives Indu.
Trap (A): Moving two seats to the right of Jatin (Seat 5) instead of one gives Kavya.
questions.verify_code:
import itertools
sols = []
for p in itertools.permutations(['Gaurav', 'Harish', 'Jatin', 'Kavya', 'Lalit']):
    s = {'Indu': 0}
    s.update({n: i + 1 for i, n in enumerate(p)})
    if s['Gaurav'] != (s['Indu'] + 2) % 6: continue
    if (s['Kavya'] - s['Gaurav']) % 6 != 3: continue
    if s['Harish'] != (s['Kavya'] - 1) % 6: continue
    if (s['Jatin'] - s['Indu']) % 6 in (1, 5): continue
    sols.append(s)
assert len(sols) == 1
inv = {v: k for k, v in sols[0].items()}
answer = inv[(sols[0]['Jatin'] + 1) % 6]

questions.question_text: Five chartered accountants—Manish, Nidhi, Omkar, Pooja, and Qasim—are sitting in a row facing South. Pooja sits at the extreme left end of the row (from their own South-facing perspective). Manish sits second to the right of Pooja. Only one person sits between Manish and Qasim. Nidhi sits to the immediate left of Manish. Who sits to the immediate right of Manish?
questions.trap_type: Mixing up own left/right for South-facing people or counting the wrong number of seats
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: Everyone faces South, so use their own left and right. Number the five seats 0 to 4 from their own left to their own right (this is right to left for a viewer facing them). 1) Pooja sits at the extreme left end, so Pooja is at Seat 0. 2) Manish sits second to the right of Pooja, so Manish is at Seat 2. 3) Only one person sits between Manish and Qasim; Seat 0 is taken, so Qasim is at Seat 4. 4) Nidhi sits to the immediate left of Manish, so Nidhi is at Seat 1. 5) Omkar takes the remaining Seat 3. Order from their own left to right: Pooja, Nidhi, Manish, Omkar, Qasim. The immediate right of Manish is Seat 3, which is Omkar.
Trap (B): Taking the immediate left of Manish instead of the immediate right gives Nidhi.
Trap (C): Moving two seats to the right of Manish instead of one gives Qasim.
Trap (A): Moving two seats to the left of Manish instead of one to the right gives Pooja.
questions.verify_code:
import itertools
sols = []
for p in itertools.permutations(['Manish', 'Nidhi', 'Omkar', 'Pooja', 'Qasim']):
    s = {n: i for i, n in enumerate(p)}
    if s['Pooja'] != 0: continue
    if s['Manish'] != s['Pooja'] + 2: continue
    if abs(s['Manish'] - s['Qasim']) != 2: continue
    if s['Nidhi'] != s['Manish'] - 1: continue
    sols.append(p)
assert len(sols) == 1
p = sols[0]
answer = p[p.index('Manish') + 1]

questions.concept_tag: Circular Seating Arrangement - Six People Facing Outward
questions.question_text: Six professors—Raghav, Suman, Tarun, Urvashi, Vikas, and Waseem—sit around a circular table facing outward (away from the center). Suman sits third to the right of Raghav. Tarun sits to the immediate left of Suman. Vikas sits second to the right of Tarun. Waseem sits to the immediate right of Raghav. Who sits directly opposite to Urvashi?
questions.trap_type: Selecting the immediate neighbour instead of the opposite person in a 6-seat circle
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: For people facing outward, 'right' is clockwise. Number the six seats 0 to 5 clockwise, so moving right is +1 and moving left is -1. 1) Place Raghav at Seat 0. 2) Suman sits third to the right of Raghav, so Suman is at Seat 3 (opposite Raghav). 3) Tarun sits to the immediate left of Suman, so Tarun is at Seat 2. 4) Vikas sits second to the right of Tarun, so Vikas is at Seat 4. 5) Waseem sits to the immediate right of Raghav, so Waseem is at Seat 1, and Urvashi takes the remaining Seat 5. In a 6-seat circle, the person opposite Seat 5 is at Seat (5 + 3) % 6 = 2, which is Tarun.
Trap (C): Taking the immediate left of Urvashi (Seat 4) instead of the person opposite gives Vikas.
Trap (D): Moving only two seats from Urvashi (Seat 1) instead of three gives Waseem.
Trap (A): Taking the immediate right of Urvashi (Seat 0) instead of the person opposite gives Raghav.
questions.verify_code:
import itertools
sols = []
for p in itertools.permutations(['Suman', 'Tarun', 'Urvashi', 'Vikas', 'Waseem']):
    s = {'Raghav': 0}
    s.update({n: i + 1 for i, n in enumerate(p)})
    if s['Suman'] != (s['Raghav'] + 3) % 6: continue
    if s['Tarun'] != (s['Suman'] - 1) % 6: continue
    if s['Vikas'] != (s['Tarun'] + 2) % 6: continue
    if s['Waseem'] != (s['Raghav'] + 1) % 6: continue
    sols.append(s)
assert len(sols) == 1
inv = {v: k for k, v in sols[0].items()}
answer = inv[(sols[0]['Urvashi'] + 3) % 6]

questions.question_text:
Statements:
1. Only a few mangoes are apples.
2. All apples are bananas.
3. No banana is a cherry.
Conclusions:
I. Some mangoes are definitely not apples.
II. Some mangoes are not cherries.
Which of the following options is correct?

options.B: Both Conclusions I and II follow
options.D: Neither Conclusion I nor II follows

questions.trap_type: Treating 'Only a few A are B' as ordinary 'Some A are B' and ignoring the 'Some A are not B' part
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: 1) 'Only a few mangoes are apples' means BOTH 'Some mangoes are apples' AND 'Some mangoes are not apples'. Therefore, Conclusion I ('Some mangoes are definitely not apples') directly follows. 2) Since some mangoes are apples, and all apples are bananas, those specific mangoes are also bananas. Because no banana is a cherry, the part of mangoes that lies inside apples (and bananas) can never be cherries. Therefore, Conclusion II ('Some mangoes are not cherries') also definitely follows. Hence, both Conclusions I and II follow.
Trap (C): Failing to chain 'Some mangoes are apples' with 'All apples are bananas' and 'No banana is a cherry' leads to rejecting Conclusion II and picking Only Conclusion I follows.
Trap (A): Treating 'Only a few mangoes are apples' as a standard 'Some mangoes are apples' (where 'All mangoes are apples' would be possible, making 'Some mangoes are not apples' doubtful) leads to rejecting Conclusion I and picking Only Conclusion II follows.
Trap (D): Rejecting both negative conclusions under the false rule that positive statements cannot yield 'some... not' conclusions leads to Neither follows.
questions.verify_code:
import itertools
SETS = ['M', 'A', 'B', 'C']
regions = [r for r in itertools.product([0, 1], repeat=len(SETS)) if any(r)]
def models():
    for occ in itertools.product([0, 1], repeat=len(regions)):
        live = [r for r, o in zip(regions, occ) if o]
        if all(any(r[i] for r in live) for i in range(len(SETS))):
            yield live
ix = {n: i for i, n in enumerate(SETS)}
some = lambda m, a, b: any(r[ix[a]] and r[ix[b]] for r in m)
some_not = lambda m, a, b: any(r[ix[a]] and not r[ix[b]] for r in m)
all_ = lambda m, a, b: not some_not(m, a, b)
no = lambda m, a, b: not some(m, a, b)
few = lambda m, a, b: some(m, a, b) and some_not(m, a, b)
ms = [m for m in models() if few(m, 'M', 'A') and all_(m, 'A', 'B') and no(m, 'B', 'C')]
c1, c2 = lambda m: some_not(m, 'M', 'A'), lambda m: some_not(m, 'M', 'C')
f1 = any(c1(m) for m in ms) if False else all(c1(m) for m in ms)
f2 = any(c2(m) for m in ms) if False else all(c2(m) for m in ms)
answer = {(True, False): 'Only Conclusion I follows', (False, True): 'Only Conclusion II follows', (True, True): 'Both Conclusions I and II follow', (False, False): 'Neither Conclusion I nor II follows'}[(f1, f2)]

questions.concept_tag: Syllogism - Only a Few & All Possibility Trap
questions.question_text:
Statements:
1. Only a few rivers are lakes.
2. Some lakes are oceans.
Conclusions:
I. All rivers being lakes is a possibility.
II. All lakes being rivers is a possibility.
Which of the following options is correct?

options.A: Both Conclusions I and II follow
options.B: Neither Conclusion I nor II follows

questions.trap_type: Symmetrical restriction error on 'Only a few A are B'
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: The statement 'Only a few rivers are lakes' imposes a strict restriction on the subject ('rivers'): some rivers are lakes, and some rivers are definitely NOT lakes. Because some rivers are definitely not lakes, the entire set of rivers can NEVER go inside lakes—making Conclusion I ('All rivers being lakes is a possibility') false. However, the restriction applies only from rivers to lakes, not from lakes to rivers. The entire circle of 'lakes' can sit completely inside part of the 'rivers' circle while leaving other rivers outside lakes. Thus, Conclusion II ('All lakes being rivers is a possibility') is true. Only Conclusion II follows.
Trap (D): Reversing the direction of the 'Only a few' restriction (thinking all rivers can be lakes, but not all lakes can be rivers) gives Only Conclusion I follows.
Trap (A): Treating 'Only a few' as a simple 'Some' statement (where 'All' is possible in both directions) gives Both Conclusions I and II follow.
Trap (B): Assuming 'Only a few rivers are lakes' forbids 'All' possibilities in both directions (symmetrical restriction error) gives Neither Conclusion I nor II follows.
questions.verify_code:
import itertools
SETS = ['R', 'L', 'O']
regions = [r for r in itertools.product([0, 1], repeat=len(SETS)) if any(r)]
def models():
    for occ in itertools.product([0, 1], repeat=len(regions)):
        live = [r for r, o in zip(regions, occ) if o]
        if all(any(r[i] for r in live) for i in range(len(SETS))):
            yield live
ix = {n: i for i, n in enumerate(SETS)}
some = lambda m, a, b: any(r[ix[a]] and r[ix[b]] for r in m)
some_not = lambda m, a, b: any(r[ix[a]] and not r[ix[b]] for r in m)
all_ = lambda m, a, b: not some_not(m, a, b)
no = lambda m, a, b: not some(m, a, b)
few = lambda m, a, b: some(m, a, b) and some_not(m, a, b)
ms = [m for m in models() if few(m, 'R', 'L') and some(m, 'L', 'O')]
c1, c2 = lambda m: all_(m, 'R', 'L'), lambda m: all_(m, 'L', 'R')
f1 = any(c1(m) for m in ms) if True else all(c1(m) for m in ms)
f2 = any(c2(m) for m in ms) if True else all(c2(m) for m in ms)
answer = {(True, False): 'Only Conclusion I follows', (False, True): 'Only Conclusion II follows', (True, True): 'Both Conclusions I and II follow', (False, False): 'Neither Conclusion I nor II follows'}[(f1, f2)]

questions.question_text:
Statements: P >= Q = R > S; R <= T < U
Conclusions:
I. P > S
II. Q < U
Which of the following options is correct?

options.C: Both Conclusions I and II are true
options.D: Neither Conclusion I nor II is true

questions.trap_type: Missing the substitution of equal elements (Q = R) across comma-separated statements
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: 1) For Conclusion I (P > S): Trace the path from P to S in the first statement: P >= Q = R > S. Since the chain has >=, =, and strictly >, the strict inequality (>) dominates, making P > S definitely true. 2) For Conclusion II (Q < U): Combine the two statements via the common element R: Q = R <= T < U. Since the chain from Q to U has =, <=, and strictly <, the strict inequality (<) dominates, making Q < U definitely true. Therefore, both Conclusions I and II are true.
Trap (A): Seeing opposing signs between the two statements (>= in the first and <= in the second) and assuming Q and U cannot be compared without noticing that Q = R starts to the left of <= T < U gives Only Conclusion I is true.
Trap (B): Misreading P >= Q = R > S as requiring >= between P and S gives Only Conclusion II is true.
Trap (D): Requiring every symbol in the chain to be strictly > or < for a strict conclusion to hold gives Neither is true.

questions.question_text:
In a certain code language:
'X @ Y' means 'X is greater than Y'
'X # Y' means 'X is greater than or equal to Y'
'X $ Y' means 'X is equal to Y'
'X % Y' means 'X is smaller than Y'
Statements: A # B $ C @ D; C % E
Conclusions:
I. A @ D
II. E @ D
Which of the following options is correct?

options.B: Both Conclusions I and II are true
options.D: Neither Conclusion I nor II is true

questions.trap_type: Reversing the inequality direction when linking a reversed branch (C < E vs C > D)
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: Decode the symbols first: @ means >, # means >=, $ means =, and % means <. Now rewrite the statements: A >= B = C > D and C < E (which is equivalent to E > C). 1) Check Conclusion I (A @ D, i.e., A > D): From A >= B = C > D, the strict '>' dominates, so A > D is definitely true. 2) Check Conclusion II (E @ D, i.e., E > D): Combine E > C and C > D to get E > C > D, which means E > D is also definitely true. Thus, both Conclusions I and II are true.
Trap (C): Seeing C > D and C < E with opposite-facing signs (< and >) and assuming E and D have a blocked relation (forgetting to flip C < E into E > C before chaining with C > D) gives Only Conclusion I is true.
Trap (A): Misreading # (>=) as % (<) in the first statement blocks A > D and gives Only Conclusion II is true.
Trap (D): Reading '@' as 'smaller than' in both conclusions (A < D and E < D) makes both false, giving Neither Conclusion I nor II is true.

questions.question_text: If 'A + B' means 'A is the father of B', 'A - B' means 'A is the mother of B', 'A * B' means 'A is the brother of B', and 'A / B' means 'A is the sister of B', then how is Kartik related to Meera in the expression 'Kartik * Lata - Meera'?
questions.trap_type: Confusing Maternal Uncle with Paternal Uncle or reversing the direction of relation
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: Break the expression 'Kartik * Lata - Meera' into two segments: 1) 'Kartik * Lata' means Kartik is the brother of Lata (so Kartik is male, and Kartik and Lata are siblings). 2) 'Lata - Meera' means Lata is the mother of Meera (so Lata is female, one generation above Meera). Since Kartik is the brother of Meera's mother (Lata), Kartik is the Maternal Uncle of Meera.
Trap (A): Identifying Kartik as an uncle correctly but misreading '-' as 'father of' instead of 'mother of' gives Paternal Uncle.
Trap (D): Ignoring the generation gap created by '-' and treating all three people as siblings in the same generation gives Brother.
Trap (B): Answering how Meera is related to Kartik (the reverse direction) instead of how Kartik is related to Meera gives Niece.

questions.concept_tag: Coded Blood Relations - In-Law & Spousal Chain
questions.question_text:
In a certain code language:
'P @ Q' means 'P is the wife of Q'
'P # Q' means 'P is the son of Q'
'P $ Q' means 'P is the sister of Q'
In the expression 'Ritu $ Sameer # Tanuja @ Umesh', how is Umesh related to Ritu?
questions.trap_type: Misreading the spouse code '@' or answering for the wrong person
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: Decode the expression one link at a time. 1) 'Ritu $ Sameer' means Ritu is the sister of Sameer, so Ritu and Sameer are siblings. 2) 'Sameer # Tanuja' means Sameer is the son of Tanuja, so Tanuja is the parent of Sameer and Ritu. 3) 'Tanuja @ Umesh' means Tanuja is the wife of Umesh, so Tanuja is their mother and Umesh is her husband. Umesh is the husband of Ritu's mother, so Umesh is the Father of Ritu.
Trap (A): Answering Tanuja's relation to Ritu instead of Umesh's gives Mother.
Trap (D): Reading '@' as 'mother of' makes Umesh another child of Tanuja, giving Brother.
Trap (B): Reading '@' as 'sister of' makes Umesh the brother of Ritu's mother, giving Maternal Uncle.

questions.concept_tag: Coded Blood Relations - Backward/Reversed Operand Coding
questions.question_text:
Read the following information carefully:
'M & N' means 'N is the father of M'
'M % N' means 'N is the mother of M'
'M ^ N' means 'N is the husband of M'
In the expression 'Pooja % Rekha & Suresh', how is Suresh related to Pooja?
questions.trap_type: Reading backward-coded definitions ('N is the father of M') as forward-coded ('M is the father of N')
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: Notice carefully that every rule defines the SECOND person (N) in terms of the FIRST person (M): 1) In 'Pooja % Rekha', the rule 'M % N means N is the mother of M' tells us that Rekha is the mother of Pooja. 2) In 'Rekha & Suresh', the rule 'M & N means N is the father of M' tells us that Suresh is the father of Rekha. Since Rekha is Pooja's mother and Suresh is Rekha's father, Suresh is the Maternal Grandfather of Pooja.
Trap (B): Skipping the intermediate generation (Rekha) and linking Suresh directly as the parent of Pooja gives Father.
Trap (C): Reading '%' forward ('Pooja is the mother of Rekha') while reading '&' correctly makes Pooja and Suresh the two parents of Rekha, giving Husband.
Trap (A): Identifying the two-generation gap correctly (grandfather) but misreading '%' as 'father of' instead of 'mother of' gives Paternal Grandfather.

questions.concept_tag: Direction Sense - Pythagorean Shortest Distance & Direction
questions.question_text: Vikram starts walking from Point A and walks 12 m North to reach Point B. From Point B, he turns right and walks 9 m to reach Point C. From Point C, he turns right again and walks 4 m to reach Point D. Finally, he turns left and walks 6 m to reach Point E. What is the shortest distance between Point A and Point E, and in which direction is Point E with respect to Point A?
questions.trap_type: Turning left from South as West instead of East, or reversing reference point
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: Place Point A at the origin (0, 0). 1) 12 m North takes Vikram to Point B (0, 12). 2) Turning right from North is East; walking 9 m East takes him to Point C (9, 12). 3) Turning right from East is South; walking 4 m South takes him to Point D (9, 8). 4) Turning left when facing South means turning East; walking 6 m East takes him to Point E (9 + 6, 8) = (15, 8). Now compute the shortest (straight-line) distance from A (0, 0) to E (15, 8) using the Pythagoras theorem: sqrt(15 * 15 + 8 * 8) = sqrt(225 + 64) = sqrt(289) = 17 m. Since x = +15 (East) and y = +8 (North), Point E is in the North-East direction with respect to Point A.
Trap (D): Calculating the distance (17 m) correctly but finding the direction of Point A with respect to Point E (instead of E with respect to A) gives 17 m, South-West.
Trap (A): Adding the net horizontal and vertical components (15 m + 8 m = 23 m) instead of using the Pythagorean theorem gives 23 m, North-East.
Trap (B): Stopping at Point C (sqrt(12 * 12 + 9 * 9) = 15 m) or taking only the horizontal displacement (15 m) gives 15 m, North-East.
questions.verify_code:
x, y = 0, 0
d = (0, 1)
right = lambda v: (v[1], -v[0])
left = lambda v: (-v[1], v[0])
x, y = x + 12 * d[0], y + 12 * d[1]
d = right(d); x, y = x + 9 * d[0], y + 9 * d[1]
d = right(d); x, y = x + 4 * d[0], y + 4 * d[1]
d = left(d); x, y = x + 6 * d[0], y + 6 * d[1]
dist = round((x * x + y * y) ** 0.5)
assert dist * dist == x * x + y * y and x > 0 and y > 0
ans = str(dist) + ' m, North-East'
OPTS = {'C': '17 m, North-East', 'D': '17 m, South-West', 'A': '23 m, North-East', 'B': '15 m, North-East'}
answer = [k for k, v in OPTS.items() if v == ans][0]

questions.concept_tag: Direction Sense - Rectangular Loop & Distance Calculation
questions.question_text: Ananya leaves her office and walks 15 m West to reach a bus stop. She then turns left and walks 20 m to reach a café. From the café, she turns left again and walks 27 m to reach a bookstore. Finally, she turns left and walks 25 m to reach her home. What is the shortest distance between her office and her home?
questions.trap_type: Adding instead of subtracting opposite parallel movements before applying Pythagoras
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: Set the office at the origin (0, 0). 1) Walking 15 m West reaches the bus stop at (-15, 0). 2) Turning left from West is South; walking 20 m South reaches the café at (-15, -20). 3) Turning left from South is East; walking 27 m East reaches the bookstore at (-15 + 27, -20) = (12, -20). 4) Turning left from East is North; walking 25 m North reaches her home at (12, -20 + 25) = (12, 5). Thus, her home is 12 m East and 5 m North of her office (0, 0). By the Pythagoras theorem, the shortest distance is sqrt(12 * 12 + 5 * 5) = sqrt(144 + 25) = sqrt(169) = 13 m.
Trap (B): Adding the horizontal and vertical net displacements (12 m + 5 m) instead of computing the hypotenuse gives 17 m.
Trap (D): Calculating only the horizontal displacement (27 - 15 = 12 m) and ignoring the 5 m vertical difference between 25 m North and 20 m South gives 12 m.
Trap (C): Subtracting the net vertical distance from the net horizontal distance (12 m - 5 m) gives 7 m.

d = left(d); x, y = x + 27 * d[0], y + 27 * d[1]

assert dist * dist == x * x + y * y

questions.concept_tag: Coding-Decoding - New Pattern (Length, Symbol, Last Letter Shift)
questions.question_text:
In a certain code language:
'TIGER' is coded as '5#S'
'MONKEY' is coded as '6@Z'
'LION' is coded as '4@O'
Based on the same coding pattern, how will 'TRAIN' be coded in that language?
questions.trap_type: Taking the symbol from the wrong example or forgetting the +1 shift on the last letter
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: Analyze the three elements (Number, Symbol, Letter) of each code: 1) Number: 'TIGER' has 5 letters -> 5; 'MONKEY' has 6 letters -> 6; 'LION' has 4 letters -> 4. So the number represents the total number of letters in the word. For 'TRAIN', the length is 5. 2) Symbol: 'TIGER' (odd length, 5) has '#'; 'MONKEY' (even length, 6) and 'LION' (even length, 4) have '@'. Since 'TRAIN' has 5 letters (odd), its symbol is '#'. 3) Letter: Last letter of TIGER is R -> R + 1 = S; last letter of MONKEY is Y -> Y + 1 = Z; last letter of LION is N -> N + 1 = O. For 'TRAIN', the last letter is N, and N + 1 = O. Combining all three gives '5#O'.
Trap (C): Copying the symbol from LION, the example whose last letter N matches TRAIN's, instead of using the odd/even word-length rule gives 5@O.
Trap (B): Keeping the last letter 'N' unchanged instead of shifting it forward by +1 gives 5#N.
Trap (A): Shifting the last letter backward by -1 (N - 1 = M) instead of forward by +1 gives 5#M.

questions.question_text: In a certain code language, 'SMART' is written as 'HNZIG' and 'BRAIN' is written as 'YIZRM'. How will 'CLOUD' be written in that language?
questions.trap_type: Missing that the middle letters L and O swap into each other's place under the opposite-letter rule
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: Observe the relation between each letter and its code using standard alphabetical positions (A=1 to Z=26): S(19)+H(8)=27, M(13)+N(14)=27, A(1)+Z(26)=27, R(18)+I(9)=27, T(20)+G(7)=27. Every letter is replaced by its reverse-alphabetical opposite pair (two letters whose positions sum to 27). Applying this rule to 'CLOUD': C(3) -> 24(X), L(12) -> 15(O), O(15) -> 12(L), U(21) -> 6(F), D(4) -> 23(W). Therefore, 'CLOUD' is coded as 'XOLFW'.
Trap (C): Miscalculating the opposite of D(4) as Z(26) instead of W(23) gives XOLFZ.
Trap (D): Applying a +1 shift to every letter (as M becomes N in SMART) instead of the opposite-letter rule gives DMPVE.
Trap (B): Leaving L and O in their original places, because L and O are each other's opposites, instead of replacing each letter gives XLOFW.
questions.verify_code:
opp = lambda w: ''.join(chr(155 - ord(c)) for c in w)
assert opp('SMART') == 'HNZIG' and opp('BRAIN') == 'YIZRM'
answer = opp('CLOUD')

questions.concept_tag: Order and Ranking - Rank Interchange in a Row
questions.question_text: In a row of cadet applicants facing North, Deepak is 14th from the left end and Pranav is 19th from the right end. When they interchange their positions, Deepak becomes 23rd from the left end. What will be Pranav's new position from the right end after the interchange?
questions.trap_type: Subtracting 1 from the rank shift when transferring the increase to the second person
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: Method 1 (Direct Shift): Before the interchange, Deepak was 14th from the left; after moving to Pranav's seat, Deepak becomes 23rd from the left—an increase of 23 - 14 = +9 positions. By symmetry, Pranav's rank from the right end also increases by the exact same amount (+9): 19 + 9 = 28th. Method 2 (Via Total Persons): Since Deepak's new seat is Pranav's old seat, that seat is 23rd from the left and 19th from the right. Total persons = 23 + 19 - 1 = 41. Now Pranav is at Deepak's old seat (14th from the left), so Pranav's rank from the right is (41 - 14) + 1 = 28th.
Trap (B): Calculating the total as 41 correctly, but forgetting to add +1 when finding Pranav's right-end rank (41 - 14 = 27) gives 27th.
Trap (A): Adding 1 to the shift (19 + 9 + 1 = 29) due to confusing rank-difference formulas with total-person formulas gives 29th.
Trap (C): Stopping after calculating the total number of cadets in the row (23 + 19 - 1 = 41) gives 41st.

questions.concept_tag: Order and Ranking - Overlapping vs Non-Overlapping Row
questions.question_text: In a row of 45 students, Kritika is 18th from the left end and Roshan is 16th from the right end. How many students are sitting strictly between Kritika and Roshan?
questions.trap_type: Subtracting an extra 1 from (Total - Sum of Ranks) when calculating persons strictly between
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: First check whether the two ranks overlap by adding them: 18 (from left) + 16 (from right) = 34. Since 34 is less than the total number of students (45), it is a non-overlapping case. The number of students sitting strictly between them is simply Total - (Left Rank + Right Rank) = 45 - (18 + 16) = 45 - 34 = 11.
Trap (A): Subtracting an extra 1 from the difference (45 - 34 - 1 = 10) by confusing the 'between' formula with the 'Total = L + R - 1' formula gives 10.
Trap (D): Adding 1 to the difference (45 - 34 + 1 = 12) by confusing it with the 'Opposite Rank = Total - Rank + 1' formula gives 12.
Trap (C): Excluding Kritika and Roshan a second time (45 - 34 - 2) gives 9.

questions.question_text:
Study the following alphanumeric-symbol series carefully and answer the question below:
M 4 # P 7 @ R 2 $ K 9 % T 5 & W 8 * Z 3
Which element is sixth to the left of the fifteenth element from the left end of the above arrangement?
questions.trap_type: Off-by-one counting from a reference element, or dropping the reference element
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: When both reference directions are from the same end ('left of the ... from the left end'), subtract the two positions: 15 - 6 = 9th element from the left end. Now count to the 9th element from the left in 'M(1) 4(2) #(3) P(4) 7(5) @(6) R(7) 2(8) $(9) K(10) ...': the 9th element from the left end is '$'.
Trap (B): Counting 6 steps left from the 15th element inclusively (counting the 15th element '&' as 1 instead of 0, which lands on the 15 - 6 - 1 = 8th element) gives 2.
Trap (A): Off-by-one error to the right (landing on the 10th element instead of the 9th element) gives K.
Trap (D): Reading the question as 'sixth element from the left end' and ignoring the fifteenth-element reference gives @.
questions.verify_code:
s = 'M 4 # P 7 @ R 2 $ K 9 % T 5 & W 8 * Z 3'.split()
assert len(s) == 20 and s[14] == '&'
answer = s[15 - 6 - 1]

questions.question_text: Five friends Aarav, Bina, Chetan, Divya and Eshan live on five different floors from 1 to 5, floor 1 is bottom and floor 5 is top. Clues: Eshan lives on the topmost floor. Aarav lives on an even numbered floor but not on floor 2. Bina lives immediately above Chetan. Divya lives below Aarav. Chetan does not live on floor 1. Who lives on floor 3?
questions.trap_type: Reversing 'immediately above', dropping a negative clue, or reading the wrong floor
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: Floors are numbered 1 (bottom) to 5 (top). 1) Eshan lives on the topmost floor, so Eshan is on floor 5. 2) Aarav lives on an even floor other than 2, so Aarav is on floor 4. 3) Bina lives immediately above Chetan, so the pair (Chetan, Bina) takes two consecutive free floors among 1, 2 and 3: (1, 2) or (2, 3). Chetan does not live on floor 1, so Chetan is on floor 2 and Bina on floor 3. 4) Divya takes floor 1, which is below Aarav as required. Final order from bottom: Divya, Chetan, Bina, Aarav, Eshan. Floor 3 belongs to Bina.
Trap (B): Reading 'Bina lives immediately above Chetan' the other way round puts Chetan on floor 3 and Bina on floor 2, giving Chetan.
Trap (D): Ignoring the clue 'Chetan does not live on floor 1' puts Chetan on 1 and Bina on 2, leaving floor 3 for Divya.
Trap (A): Reading the floor one place too high (floor 4 instead of floor 3) gives Aarav.

import itertools
sols = []
for p in itertools.permutations(['Aarav', 'Bina', 'Chetan', 'Divya', 'Eshan']):
    f = {n: i + 1 for i, n in enumerate(p)}
    if f['Eshan'] != 5: continue
    if f['Aarav'] % 2 or f['Aarav'] == 2: continue
    if f['Bina'] != f['Chetan'] + 1: continue
    if f['Divya'] >= f['Aarav']: continue
    if f['Chetan'] == 1: continue
    sols.append(p)
assert len(sols) == 1
answer = sols[0][2]

questions.question_text: Five boxes belonging to Rohan, Sneha, Karan, Priya and Vikram are stacked one above another. Position 1 is the top and position 5 is the bottom. Clues: Vikram's box is at the bottom. Sneha's box is at the top. Rohan's box is immediately above Karan's box. Priya's box is below Rohan's box but not at the bottom. Karan's box is not adjacent to Vikram's box. Whose box is immediately below Karan's box?
questions.trap_type: Reversing 'immediately above' or counting the wrong number of places from the reference box
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: 1) Sneha is at position 1 and Vikram at position 5. 2) Rohan is immediately above Karan, so (Rohan, Karan) is (2, 3) or (3, 4). 3) Karan is not adjacent to Vikram, so Karan is not at 4; hence Rohan is at 2 and Karan at 3. 4) Priya is below Rohan but not at the bottom, so Priya is at 4. Stack from top: Sneha, Rohan, Karan, Priya, Vikram. The box immediately below Karan (position 4) is Priya's.
Trap (A): Reading 'Rohan is immediately above Karan' the other way round puts Karan at 2 and Rohan at 3, giving Rohan below Karan.
Trap (D): Counting two places below Karan instead of one gives position 5, Vikram.
Trap (C): Counting two places above Karan instead of one below gives position 1, Sneha.

Ananya's meeting is immediately before Farhan's meeting. Chirag's meeting is in May. Farhan's meeting is not in April. Who has the meeting in April?
questions.trap_type: Dropping the negative clue or reversing 'immediately before'
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: 1) Deepa is in January and Chirag in May, so February, March and April remain for Ananya, Bhavesh and Farhan. 2) Ananya is immediately before Farhan, so (Ananya, Farhan) is (February, March) or (March, April). 3) Farhan is not in April, so Ananya is in February and Farhan in March. 4) Bhavesh takes April. Order: Deepa, Ananya, Farhan, Bhavesh, Chirag. April belongs to Bhavesh.
Trap (D): Reading the clue the other way round (Farhan immediately before Ananya) allows Farhan in March and Ananya in April, giving Ananya.
Trap (A): Ignoring 'Farhan's meeting is not in April' allows Ananya in March and Farhan in April, giving Farhan.

questions.question_text:
Statements: No laptop is a tablet. Some tablets are phones. All phones are gadgets.
Conclusions: I. Some gadgets are tablets. II. No laptop is a phone. III. Some gadgets are not laptops.
Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.A: All of I, II and III follow

questions.trap_type: Accepting a 'No' conclusion that is only possible, or missing a conclusion reached through the tablet-gadget overlap
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: 1) Some tablets are phones and all phones are gadgets, so those tablets are gadgets: Some tablets are gadgets, which converts to Some gadgets are tablets. Conclusion I follows. 2) No laptop is a tablet says nothing about phones that are not tablets; a laptop may or may not be a phone, so 'No laptop is a phone' is only a possibility. Conclusion II does not follow. 3) The gadgets that are tablets cannot be laptops (no laptop is a tablet), so Some gadgets are not laptops. Conclusion III follows. Answer: Only I and III follow.
Trap (D): Stopping after Conclusion I and missing that the same tablet-gadgets give III gives Only I follows.
Trap (A): Treating 'No laptop is a tablet' plus 'Some tablets are phones' as 'No laptop is a phone' accepts II as well, giving All of I, II and III follow.
Trap (C): Rejecting I because the statements never mention gadgets and tablets together gives Only III follows.

import itertools
SETS = ['L', 'T', 'P', 'G']
regions = [r for r in itertools.product([0, 1], repeat=len(SETS)) if any(r)]
def models():
    for occ in itertools.product([0, 1], repeat=len(regions)):
        live = [r for r, o in zip(regions, occ) if o]
        if all(any(r[i] for r in live) for i in range(len(SETS))):
            yield live
ix = {n: i for i, n in enumerate(SETS)}
some = lambda m, a, b: any(r[ix[a]] and r[ix[b]] for r in m)
some_not = lambda m, a, b: any(r[ix[a]] and not r[ix[b]] for r in m)
all_ = lambda m, a, b: not some_not(m, a, b)
no = lambda m, a, b: not some(m, a, b)
ms = [m for m in models() if no(m, 'L', 'T') and some(m, 'T', 'P') and all_(m, 'P', 'G')]
f1 = all(some(m, 'G', 'T') for m in ms)
f2 = all(no(m, 'L', 'P') for m in ms)
f3 = all(some_not(m, 'G', 'L') for m in ms)
answer = {(True, False, True): 'Only I and III follow', (True, False, False): 'Only I follows', (True, True, True): 'All of I, II and III follow', (False, False, True): 'Only III follows'}[(f1, f2, f3)]

questions.trap_type: Off-by-one counting from an end or from the reference element, or moving the wrong way
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: Number the 20 elements from the left: M(1) 3(2) $(3) K(4) 7(5) %(6) L(7) 9(8) &(9) P(10) 2(11) #(12) Q(13) 5(14) @(15) R(16) 8(17) ^(18) S(19) 4(20). The 9th from the right end is position 20 - 9 + 1 = 12, which is #. The 4th element to the left of # is position 12 - 4 = 8, which is 9.
Trap (D): Counting # itself as the first step (inclusive counting) moves only three places and lands on position 9, giving &.
Trap (C): Moving 4 places to the right of # instead of the left lands on position 16, giving R.
Trap (B): Forgetting the +1 when converting from the right end (20 - 9 = 11) and then moving 4 left lands on position 7, giving L.
