questions.question_text:
Statement: The company has launched a new electric scooter and is advertising its range of 200 km on a single charge.
Assumptions:
I. People prefer electric scooters over petrol scooters.
II. A long range is a feature that buyers of electric scooters want.
Which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement?

options.C: Neither I nor II is implicit
options.D: Both I and II are implicit

questions.trap_type: Preference over petrol assumed, Both assumed, Neither assumed
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: An assumption is implicit only if the statement cannot make sense without it. 1) Assumption I: Launching an electric scooter needs only some demand for electric scooters; it does not need people in general to prefer them over petrol scooters. I is not implicit. 2) Assumption II: The company chooses to advertise the 200 km range, which makes sense only if buyers value a long range. II is implicit. Answer: Only II is implicit.
Trap (A): Reading the launch itself as proof that electric scooters are preferred over petrol ones accepts I instead of II.
Trap (D): Accepting the over-general preference in I along with II gives Both I and II.
Trap (C): Treating the advertisement as a plain fact with no assumption behind it rejects II as well, giving Neither.

questions.question_text: Statement: Many accidents have been reported on the highway due to large potholes. Courses of action: I. Government should get potholes repaired immediately. II. Government should ban all vehicles on the highway. Which course of action follows?
questions.trap_type: Extreme action accepted, Both extreme, No action
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: A course of action follows if it is practical and addresses the problem in the statement. 1) Course I: The accidents are caused by large potholes, so repairing them immediately removes the cause. I follows. 2) Course II: Banning all vehicles on the highway is impractical and stops all traffic instead of fixing the potholes. II does not follow. Answer: Only I follows.
Trap (B): Choosing the extreme step because it would stop all accidents gives Only II follows.
Trap (C): Accepting the ban along with the repair gives Both I and II follow.
Trap (A): Treating an immediate repair as too costly to be practical rejects I as well, giving Neither.

questions.question_text:
Statements:
I. The local administration has ordered the closure of schools for three days.
II. A severe cyclonic storm is expected to hit the coastal region.
Which of the following best describes the relation between the two statements?

options.B: Both are effects of a common cause
options.C: I is the cause and II is the effect
options.D: II is the cause and I is the effect

questions.trap_type: Reversed cause effect, Independent causes misjudgement, Common cause confusion
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: The cyclone forecast (II) is a natural event that comes first; the administration closes schools (I) to keep students safe from it. So II is the cause and I is its effect. Answer: II is the cause and I is the effect.
Trap (C): Reading the statements in their printed order (I first) reverses the direction, giving I as the cause and II as the effect.
Trap (A): Missing the safety link between the forecast and the closure treats them as unrelated, giving Both are independent causes.
Trap (B): Linking both to the season instead of to each other gives Both are effects of a common cause.

questions.question_text: If 26th January 2024 was Friday, what day of the week was 26th January 2023?
questions.trap_type: Leap year double shift, Same day assumption, Forward shift
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: 1) The leap day of 2024 is 29 February 2024, which comes after 26 January 2024, so it is not inside the period from 26 January 2023 to 26 January 2024. 2) The period therefore has 365 days = 52 weeks + 1 odd day. 3) Going back one year from Friday shifts the day back by 1, so 26 January 2023 was a Thursday.
Trap (A): Counting 29 February 2024 inside the period (2 odd days) and shifting back 2 gives Wednesday.
Trap (D): Assuming the same date falls on the same weekday every year gives Friday.
Trap (C): Shifting the odd day forward instead of backward gives Saturday.
questions.verify_code:
leap = lambda y: y % 4 == 0 and (y % 100 != 0 or y % 400 == 0)
mdays = lambda y: [31, 29 if leap(y) else 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31]
def ordinal(y, m, dd):
    return sum(366 if leap(k) else 365 for k in range(1, y)) + sum(mdays(y)[:m - 1]) + dd
days = ['Monday', 'Tuesday', 'Wednesday', 'Thursday', 'Friday', 'Saturday', 'Sunday']
gap = ordinal(2024, 1, 26) - ordinal(2023, 1, 26)
assert gap == 365
answer = days[(days.index('Friday') - gap) % 7]

questions.question_text: Seven friends Aarti, Bhavya, Chetan, Divya, Esha, Farhan and Gaurav sit in a row. Some face North and some face South. Clues: Gaurav sits at the left end and faces North. Farhan sits at the right end and faces South. Divya sits exactly in the middle of the row and faces South. Chetan sits to the immediate right of Divya and faces the same direction as Divya. Only one person sits between Chetan and Esha. Esha and Bhavya both face the same direction as Gaurav. Bhavya sits to the immediate right of Esha. Aarti faces the direction opposite to Gaurav. Who sits second to the left of Chetan?
questions.trap_type: Using the viewer's left/right for a South-facing person or counting the wrong number of seats
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: Number the seats 1 to 7 from the left end. For a North-facing person, right is towards seat 7; for a South-facing person, right is towards seat 1 and left is towards seat 7. 1) Gaurav is at seat 1 (North) and Farhan at seat 7 (South). 2) Divya is in the middle, seat 4, facing South. 3) Chetan is to Divya's immediate right; Divya faces South, so her right is seat 3. Chetan is at seat 3 and faces South. 4) Only one person sits between Chetan and Esha, so Esha is at seat 1 or seat 5; seat 1 is taken, so Esha is at seat 5, facing North. 5) Bhavya is to the immediate right of Esha, who faces North, so Bhavya is at seat 6, facing North. 6) Aarti takes seat 2 and faces South. Row from the left: Gaurav, Aarti, Chetan, Divya, Esha, Bhavya, Farhan. Chetan faces South, so his left is towards seat 7; second to his left is seat 5, Esha.
Trap (D): Using the viewer's left for Chetan (towards seat 1) instead of his own left moves to seat 1, giving Gaurav.
Trap (C): Taking the immediate left of Chetan (one seat) instead of second to the left gives seat 4, Divya.
Trap (B): Counting three seats to Chetan's left instead of two gives seat 6, Bhavya.
questions.verify_code:
import itertools
N = ['Aarti', 'Bhavya', 'Chetan', 'Divya', 'Esha', 'Farhan', 'Gaurav']
sols = []
for p in itertools.permutations(N):
    s = {n: i + 1 for i, n in enumerate(p)}
    for fc in itertools.product('NS', repeat=7):
        f = dict(zip(N, fc))
        right = lambda n, k: s[n] + k if f[n] == 'N' else s[n] - k
        if s['Gaurav'] != 1 or f['Gaurav'] != 'N': continue
        if s['Farhan'] != 7 or f['Farhan'] != 'S': continue
        if s['Divya'] != 4 or f['Divya'] != 'S': continue
        if s['Chetan'] != right('Divya', 1) or f['Chetan'] != f['Divya']: continue
        if abs(s['Chetan'] - s['Esha']) != 2: continue
        if f['Esha'] != f['Gaurav'] or f['Bhavya'] != f['Gaurav']: continue
        if s['Bhavya'] != right('Esha', 1): continue
        if f['Aarti'] == f['Gaurav']: continue
        sols.append((s, f))
assert len(sols) == 1
s, f = sols[0]
inv = {v: k for k, v in s.items()}
answer = inv[s['Chetan'] + 2 if f['Chetan'] == 'S' else s['Chetan'] - 2]

questions.question_text: Six friends Rohan, Sneha, Vikram, Priya, Karan and Ananya sit around a circular table facing the centre. Clues: Rohan sits opposite Priya. Sneha sits to the immediate left of Rohan. Vikram sits second to the right of Sneha. Ananya sits to the immediate right of Priya. Karan sits between Priya and Vikram. Who sits second to the left of Karan?
questions.trap_type: Mixing up left and right for centre-facing people or counting the wrong number of seats
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: For people facing the centre, left is clockwise and right is anticlockwise. Number the seats 0 to 5 clockwise, so left is +1 and right is -1. 1) Rohan is at seat 0 and Priya opposite at seat 3. 2) Sneha is to the immediate left of Rohan: seat 1. 3) Vikram is second to the right of Sneha: 1 - 2 = seat 5. 4) Ananya is to the immediate right of Priya: seat 2. 5) Karan takes seat 4, which lies between Priya (3) and Vikram (5). Second to the left of Karan is 4 + 2 = seat 0, Rohan.
Trap (B): Counting three seats to the left of Karan (the person opposite him) instead of two gives seat 1, Sneha.
Trap (C): Moving to the right (anticlockwise) instead of the left in the last step gives seat 2, Ananya.
Trap (A): Taking the immediate left of Karan instead of second to the left gives seat 5, Vikram.
questions.verify_code:
import itertools
sols = []
for p in itertools.permutations(['Sneha', 'Vikram', 'Priya', 'Karan', 'Ananya']):
    s = {'Rohan': 0}
    s.update({n: i + 1 for i, n in enumerate(p)})
    if (s['Priya'] - s['Rohan']) % 6 != 3: continue
    if s['Sneha'] != (s['Rohan'] + 1) % 6: continue
    if s['Vikram'] != (s['Sneha'] - 2) % 6: continue
    if s['Ananya'] != (s['Priya'] - 1) % 6: continue
    if {(s['Karan'] - s['Priya']) % 6, (s['Karan'] - s['Vikram']) % 6} != {1, 5}: continue
    sols.append(s)
assert len(sols) == 1
inv = {v: k for k, v in sols[0].items()}
answer = inv[(sols[0]['Karan'] + 2) % 6]

questions.question_text:
Statements: P > Q ≥ R < S ≤ T = U
Conclusions:
I. Q > T
II. Q ≤ T
Which of the conclusions is/are true?

options.B: Neither Conclusion I nor II is true
options.C: Either Conclusion I or II is true
options.D: Both Conclusions I and II are true

questions.trap_type: Missing the either-or rule for a complementary pair, or chaining through opposite signs
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: 1) Q and T are linked only through R: Q ≥ R and R < S ≤ T. The signs point in opposite directions at R (Q ≥ R < S), so no definite relation between Q and T can be drawn. Conclusion I (Q > T) is not definitely true and Conclusion II (Q ≤ T) is not definitely true. 2) The two conclusions involve the same pair and together cover every case (Q > T or Q ≤ T), and exactly one of them must hold. So either I or II is true.
Trap (D): Treating 'each is possible' as 'each is true' gives Both Conclusions I and II are true.
Trap (A): Chaining across the break at R as if Q ≥ R < S ≤ T gave Q ≤ T accepts II as definite, giving Only Conclusion II is true.
Trap (B): Rejecting both conclusions without checking the complementary-pair (either-or) rule gives Neither Conclusion I nor II is true.
questions.verify_code:
import itertools
V = ['P', 'Q', 'R', 'S', 'T', 'U']
ok = []
for vals in itertools.product(range(5), repeat=len(V)):
    P, Q, R, S, T, U = vals
    if P > Q >= R < S <= T == U:
        ok.append(vals)
def holds(f):
    return all(f(*v) for v in ok)
c1 = holds(lambda P, Q, R, S, T, U: Q > T)
c2 = holds(lambda P, Q, R, S, T, U: Q <= T)
either = holds(lambda P, Q, R, S, T, U: (Q > T) or (Q <= T)) and not c1 and not c2
assert any(v[1] > v[4] for v in ok) and any(v[1] <= v[4] for v in ok)
answer = 'Either Conclusion I or II is true' if either else {(True, False): 'Only Conclusion I is true', (False, True): 'Only Conclusion II is true', (True, True): 'Both Conclusions I and II are true', (False, False): 'Neither Conclusion I nor II is true'}[(c1, c2)]

questions.question_text: Six members Rajesh, Sunita, Amit, Priya, Karan and Neha are in a family. Rajesh is the father of Amit and Priya. Sunita is the wife of Rajesh. Amit is the brother of Priya. Karan is the son of Amit. Neha is the daughter of Priya. How is Karan related to Priya?
questions.trap_type: Attaching the child to the wrong parent or answering for the wrong person
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: 1) Amit and Priya are siblings (children of Rajesh and Sunita). 2) Karan is the son of Amit. 3) The son of a person's brother is that person's nephew. So Karan is the Nephew of Priya.
Trap (D): Attaching Karan to Priya instead of to Amit (Priya is Karan's aunt, not his mother) gives Son.
Trap (A): Answering Karan's relation to Neha (Priya's daughter) instead of to Priya gives Cousin.
Trap (B): Copying Amit's relation to Priya onto his son Karan gives Brother.

questions.question_text: In the evening, Sunita and Kavita are standing facing each other. Sunita's shadow falls exactly to her right. Which direction is Kavita facing?
questions.trap_type: Using the morning sun position or answering for the wrong person
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: 1) In the evening the sun is in the West, so shadows fall towards the East. 2) Sunita's shadow falls to her right, so East is on her right; a person with East on the right faces North. 3) Kavita stands facing Sunita, so Kavita faces the opposite direction, South.
Trap (D): Answering Sunita's direction instead of Kavita's gives North.
Trap (A): Taking the direction of the shadow (East) as the facing direction gives East.
Trap (B): Taking the direction of the evening sun (West) as the facing direction gives West.
questions.verify_code:
D = {'North': (0, 1), 'South': (0, -1), 'East': (1, 0), 'West': (-1, 0)}
sun = D['West']
shadow = (-sun[0], -sun[1])
right = lambda v: (v[1], -v[0])
sunita = [k for k, v in D.items() if right(v) == shadow][0]
kavita = [k for k, v in D.items() if v == (-D[sunita][0], -D[sunita][1])][0]
answer = kavita

questions.question_text:
In a certain code language:
'priya likes coffee' is written as 'ma ti na',
'coffee is hot' is written as 'na ro ko', and
'priya likes tea' is written as 'ma ti sa'.
What is the code for 'tea'?
questions.trap_type: Picking a code shared with another sentence instead of the code unique to the word
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: 1) 'priya likes' appears in the first and third sentences, and the common codes there are 'ma' and 'ti', so 'ma' and 'ti' stand for 'priya' and 'likes'. 2) 'coffee' appears in the first and second sentences, and the common code is 'na', so 'na' = coffee. 3) In the third sentence 'ma ti sa', removing 'ma' and 'ti' leaves 'sa', so 'tea' = sa.
Trap (B): Taking the first code of the third sentence gives ma, which belongs to 'priya' or 'likes'.
Trap (D): Taking the middle code of the third sentence gives ti, which belongs to 'priya' or 'likes'.
Trap (A): Taking the last code of the first sentence (where 'coffee' stands in the same place as 'tea') gives na, the code for coffee.

questions.question_text: What comes next in the series: A, C, F, J, O, ?
questions.trap_type: Repeating or skipping a gap, or applying the gap to the wrong term
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: Letter positions are A = 1, C = 3, F = 6, J = 10, O = 15. The gaps are +2, +3, +4, +5, so the next gap is +6: 15 + 6 = 21, which is U.
Trap (A): Repeating the last gap (+5) instead of increasing it gives 20, T.
Trap (D): Skipping a step and adding +7 gives 22, V.
Trap (B): Adding the next gap (+6) to J instead of to O gives 16, P.

s = 'ACFJO'
p = [ord(c) - 64 for c in s]
g = [b - a for a, b in zip(p, p[1:])]
assert g == list(range(2, 6))
answer = chr(64 + p[-1] + g[-1] + 1)

questions.question_text: In a row of 50 students facing North, Aman is 18th from the left end. What is his position from the right end?
questions.trap_type: Mishandling the +1 in end-position conversion
questions.pedagogical_explanation:

questions.question_text:
Question: Who is the youngest among P, Q and R?
Statements:
I. P is younger than Q.
II. Q is younger than R.
Which of the following is correct?

options.C: Both statements together are not sufficient
options.D: Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is sufficient

questions.trap_type: Treating one comparison as enough to rank three people
questions.pedagogical_explanation:
Step-by-step solution: 1) Statement I alone: P is younger than Q, but R could be younger than P, so I alone is not sufficient. 2) Statement II alone: Q is younger than R, but P could be younger than Q, so II alone is not sufficient. 3) Together: P is younger than Q and Q is younger than R, so P is the youngest. Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is.
Trap (A): Taking 'P is younger than Q' as proof that P is the youngest ignores R and accepts Statement I alone.
Trap (B): Taking 'Q is younger than R' as proof that Q is the youngest ignores P and accepts Statement II alone.
Trap (C): Testing each statement alone and never combining them gives Both statements together are not sufficient.
questions.verify_code:
import itertools
orders = list(itertools.permutations('PQR'))
I = lambda o: o.index('P') < o.index('Q')
II = lambda o: o.index('Q') < o.index('R')
def suff(cond):
    return len({o[0] for o in orders if cond(o)}) == 1
a, b, ab = suff(I), suff(II), suff(lambda o: I(o) and II(o))
answer = ('Statement I alone is sufficient' if a and not b else 'Statement II alone is sufficient' if b and not a else 'Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is sufficient' if ab and not a and not b else 'Both statements together are not sufficient')
